claim: Complexin regulates spontaneous and activates Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release.
source: Complexin regulates spontaneous and activates Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release, yet the molecular mechanisms are still unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement from the abstract that is supported by the broader scientific literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer experiments uncovered two conformations of complexin-1 bound to the ternary SNARE complex.
source: Here we performed single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer experiments and uncovered two conformations of complexin-1 bound to the ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the smFRET data presented in Figure 3, which shows two distinct FRET efficiency populations corresponding to two conformations.

claim: In the cis conformation, complexin-1 induces a conformational change at the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex.
source: In the cis conformation, complexin-1 induces a conformational change at the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex that specifically depends on the N-terminal, accessory, and central domains of complexin-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the smFRET data in Figure 4, showing emergence of low FRET efficiency states for SNARE label pairs at the C-terminal end upon complexin-1 addition.

claim: The conformational change induced by complexin-1 specifically depends on the N-terminal, accessory, and central domains of complexin-1.
source: In the cis conformation, complexin-1 induces a conformational change at the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex that specifically depends on the N-terminal, accessory, and central domains of complexin-1.
evidence: This is supported by truncation experiments shown in Figure 4G-I, where deletion of N-terminal or accessory domains abolished the conformational change.

claim: In the trans conformation, complexin-1 can simultaneously interact with a ternary SNARE complex via the central domain and a binary SNARE complex via the accessory domain.
source: In the trans conformation, complexin-1 can simultaneously interact with a ternary SNARE complex via the central domain and a binary SNARE complex consisting of syntaxin-1A and SNAP-25A via the accessory domain.
evidence: This is supported by the binding experiments in Figure 6, showing that complexin-1 bound to ternary SNARE complex can interact with binary SNARE complex.

claim: The cis conformation may be involved in activation of synchronous neurotransmitter release.
source: The cis conformation may be involved in activation of synchronous neurotransmitter release, whereas both conformations may be involved in regulating spontaneous release.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and prior knowledge about complexin function.

claim: Both conformations may be involved in regulating spontaneous release.
source: The cis conformation may be involved in activation of synchronous neurotransmitter release, whereas both conformations may be involved in regulating spontaneous release.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and prior knowledge about complexin function.

claim: Synchronous Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release depends critically on complexin.
source: Synchronous Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release depends critically on complexin (McMahon et al., 1995), and this activating role of complexin is conserved across all species and different types of Ca2+-induced exocytosis studied to date (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Xue et al., 2008; Maximov et al., 2009; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Cao et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The activating role of complexin is conserved across all species and different types of Ca2+-induced exocytosis studied to date.
source: Synchronous Ca2+-triggered neurotransmitter release depends critically on complexin (McMahon et al., 1995), and this activating role of complexin is conserved across all species and different types of Ca2+-induced exocytosis studied to date (Reim et al., 2001; Huntwork and Littleton, 2007; Xue et al., 2008; Maximov et al., 2009; Hobson et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Cao et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila, spontaneous release increases with knockout of complexin.
source: Complexin also regulates spontaneous release, although this effect is less conserved among species and experimental conditions: for example, in Drosophila spontaneous release increases with knockout of complexin (Xue et al., 2009; Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies in Drosophila.

claim: Knockdown of complexin in cultured cortical neurons increases spontaneous release.
source: Likewise, knockdown in cultured cortical neurons increases spontaneous release, although knockout of complexin in mice differently affects spontaneous release depending on the particular neuronal cell type (Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Knockout of complexin in mice differently affects spontaneous release depending on the particular neuronal cell type.
source: Likewise, knockdown in cultured cortical neurons increases spontaneous release, although knockout of complexin in mice differently affects spontaneous release depending on the particular neuronal cell type (Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2013; Trimbuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The primary sequence of complexin-1 is highly conserved (96%) in mouse, rat, and human.
source: We study here the homolog complexin-1 of the mammalian complexin family whose primary sequence is highly conserved (96%) in mouse, rat, and human.
evidence: This is a statement of known sequence conservation.

claim: Complexin-1 binds with high affinity (~10 nM) to the neuronal ternary SNARE complex.
source: Complexin-1 binds with high affinity (~10 nM) to the neuronal ternary SNARE complex consisting of synaptobrevin-2, syntaxin-1A, and SNAP-25A (McMahon et al., 1995; Chen et al., 2002; Pabst et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The N-terminal domain (amino acid range 1–27) of complexin-1 is required for activation of synchronous Ca2+-triggered release.
source: Complexin consists of four domains (Figure 1A): the N-terminal domain (amino acid range 1–27) is required for activation of synchronous Ca2+-triggered release, the accessory domain (amino acid range 28–48) is required for regulation of spontaneous release, the central domain (amino acid range 49–70) is required for all functions of complexin-1, and the C-terminal domain (amino acid range 71–134) is involved in vesicle priming and binds to anionic membranes with curvature sensitivity (Chen et al., 2002; Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Snead et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The accessory domain (amino acid range 28–48) of complexin-1 is required for regulation of spontaneous release.
source: Complexin consists of four domains (Figure 1A): the N-terminal domain (amino acid range 1–27) is required for activation of synchronous Ca2+-triggered release, the accessory domain (amino acid range 28–48) is required for regulation of spontaneous release, the central domain (amino acid range 49–70) is required for all functions of complexin-1, and the C-terminal domain (amino acid range 71–134) is involved in vesicle priming and binds to anionic membranes with curvature sensitivity (Chen et al., 2002; Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Snead et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The central domain (amino acid range 49–70) of complexin-1 is required for all functions of complexin-1.
source: Complexin consists of four domains (Figure 1A): the N-terminal domain (amino acid range 1–27) is required for activation of synchronous Ca2+-triggered release, the accessory domain (amino acid range 28–48) is required for regulation of spontaneous release, the central domain (amino acid range 49–70) is required for all functions of complexin-1, and the C-terminal domain (amino acid range 71–134) is involved in vesicle priming and binds to anionic membranes with curvature sensitivity (Chen et al., 2002; Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Snead et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The C-terminal domain (amino acid range 71–134) of complexin-1 is involved in vesicle priming and binds to anionic membranes with curvature sensitivity.
source: Complexin consists of four domains (Figure 1A): the N-terminal domain (amino acid range 1–27) is required for activation of synchronous Ca2+-triggered release, the accessory domain (amino acid range 28–48) is required for regulation of spontaneous release, the central domain (amino acid range 49–70) is required for all functions of complexin-1, and the C-terminal domain (amino acid range 71–134) is involved in vesicle priming and binds to anionic membranes with curvature sensitivity (Chen et al., 2002; Maximov et al., 2009; Kaeser-Woo et al., 2012; Snead et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The key roles of the four domains of complexin-1 have been reproduced in a reconstituted single vesicle fusion system.
source: The key roles of the four domains of complexin-1 have been reproduced in a reconstituted single vesicle fusion system with neuronal SNAREs, synaptotagmin-1, and complexin-1 (Lai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The regulatory effect on spontaneous fusion and the activating role on Ca2+-triggered release are governed by distinct molecular mechanisms involving different subsets of the four domains of complexin-1.
source: By varying the complexin-1 concentration, this in vitro study suggested that the regulatory effect on spontaneous fusion and the activating role on Ca2+-triggered release are governed by distinct molecular mechanisms involving different subsets of the four domains of complexin-1.
evidence: This is an inference from prior in vitro studies.

claim: The accessory domain is entirely dispensable for activation of Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: Recent in vitro experiments revealed that the accessory domain is entirely dispensable for activation of Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion, although it is essential for regulation of spontaneous release (Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The accessory domain is essential for regulation of spontaneous release.
source: Recent in vitro experiments revealed that the accessory domain is entirely dispensable for activation of Ca2+-triggered synaptic vesicle fusion, although it is essential for regulation of spontaneous release (Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Genetic experiments in Drosophila suggest distinct mechanisms for activation of Ca2+-triggered release and regulation of spontaneous release.
source: Similarly, genetic experiments in Drosophila also suggest distinct mechanisms for activation of Ca2+-triggered release and regulation of spontaneous release (Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The central domain of complexin-1 binds to the groove formed by the synaptobrevin-2 and syntaxin-1A α-helices in the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex.
source: The central domain of complexin-1 binds to the groove formed by the synaptobrevin-2 and syntaxin-1A α-helices in the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex (PDB ID 1KIL) (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a crystal structure.

claim: The interaction between the central domain of complexin-1 and the SNARE complex is antiparallel.
source: This interaction is antiparallel, i.e., the direction of the α-helix of the accessory domain of complexin-1 is antiparallel to the direction of the α-helices in the ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure cited.

claim: Complexin-1 may inhibit full ternary SNARE complex formation by preventing the C-terminal part of synaptobrevin-2 from binding to the syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A components.
source: Functional studies, along with molecular modeling suggested that complexin-1 may inhibit full ternary SNARE complex formation by preventing the C-terminal part of synaptobrevin-2 from binding to the syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A components of the ternary SNARE complex (Giraudo et al., 2006, 2009).
evidence: This is a model proposed in prior literature.

claim: A crystal structure of the 'superclamp' mutant of complexin-1 in complex with a partially truncated SNARE complex found that complexin-1 bridges two partially truncated SNARE complexes.
source: However, a subsequent crystal structure of the 'superclamp' mutant of complexin-1 (D27L, E34F, R37A) (Figure 1A) in complex with a partially truncated SNARE complex (containing a truncated synaptobrevin-2 fragment, amino acid range 25–60), along with isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and light scattering experiments instead found that complexin-1 bridges two partially truncated SNARE complexes: one partial SNARE complex binds to the central domain of complexin-1 while another partial SNARE complex weakly binds to the accessory domain of the same complexin-1 molecule (PDB IDs 3RK3 and 3RL0) (Kümmel et al., 2011; Krishnakumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures and biophysical experiments.

claim: The weak interaction of the accessory domain with a second SNARE complex was not observable by NMR.
source: However, this weak interaction of the accessory domain was not observable by NMR (Trimbuch et al., 2014), and its relevance has been debated (Trimbuch et al., 2014; Krishnakumar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: The complexin-1 superclamp mutant slightly decreased the mEPSC frequency in rescue experiments with complexin knockdown in cultured neurons.
source: For example, in rescue experiments with complexin knockdown in cultured neurons, the complexin-1 superclamp mutant slightly decreased the mEPSC (miniature excitatory postsynaptic current) frequency, while a 'poor-clamp' mutant (K26E, L41K, E47K) of complexin increased the mEPSC frequency compared to wildtype control (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neuronal studies.

claim: A 'poor-clamp' mutant of complexin increased the mEPSC frequency compared to wildtype control.
source: For example, in rescue experiments with complexin knockdown in cultured neurons, the complexin-1 superclamp mutant slightly decreased the mEPSC (miniature excitatory postsynaptic current) frequency, while a 'poor-clamp' mutant (K26E, L41K, E47K) of complexin increased the mEPSC frequency compared to wildtype control (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neuronal studies.

claim: Genetic rescue experiments in Drosophila showed that the superclamp mutant decreased spontaneous release.
source: Similarly, genetic rescue experiments in Drosophila showed that the superclamp mutant decreased spontaneous release, whereas the no-clamp mutant (L41E, A44E, A30E, A31E) (Figure 1A) slightly increased spontaneous release (Cho et al., 2014) compared to wildtype control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: The no-clamp mutant slightly increased spontaneous release compared to wildtype control in Drosophila.
source: Similarly, genetic rescue experiments in Drosophila showed that the superclamp mutant decreased spontaneous release, whereas the no-clamp mutant (L41E, A44E, A30E, A31E) (Figure 1A) slightly increased spontaneous release (Cho et al., 2014) compared to wildtype control.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: Introduction of a helix breaking mutation into the accessory domain of complexin increased spontaneous release in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, introduction of a helix breaking mutation into the accessory domain of complexin increased spontaneous release in C. elegans (Radoff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior studies in C. elegans.

claim: The dN-SB method nearly eliminated the low FRET efficiency states observed during SNARE complex assembly.
source: Remarkably, this method nearly eliminated the low FRET efficiency states and the resulting smFRET histograms consisted mainly of one high FRET efficiency state (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the smFRET data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The presence of the dN-SB fragment during ternary SNARE complex assembly prevents improper syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations.
source: Our single molecule experiments now provide an explanation of why C-terminal peptides of synaptobrevin produce more SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion when incubating binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complexes with such peptides prior to trans SNARE complex formation (Melia et al., 2002; Pobbati et al., 2006; Hernandez et al., 2012): the presence of the dN-SB fragment during ternary SNARE complex assembly prevents improper syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations which are probably not fusogenic.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in Figure 2 combined with prior literature.

claim: Improper syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations are probably not fusogenic.
source: Our single molecule experiments now provide an explanation of why C-terminal peptides of synaptobrevin produce more SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion when incubating binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complexes with such peptides prior to trans SNARE complex formation (Melia et al., 2002; Pobbati et al., 2006; Hernandez et al., 2012): the presence of the dN-SB fragment during ternary SNARE complex assembly prevents improper syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations which are probably not fusogenic.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data and prior literature.

claim: Two populations with low and high FRET efficiency were observed with means corresponding to 0.19 ± 0.12 and 0.83 ± 0.15, respectively, when measuring FRET between complexin-1 and syntaxin-1A.
source: We observed two populations with low and high FRET efficiency, with their means corresponding to 0.19 ± 0.12 and 0.83 ± 0.15, respectively (Figure 3B and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the smFRET data shown in Figure 3B and Table 1.

claim: The calculated FRET efficiency from the crystal structure PDB ID 1KIL is 0.49 for the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex.
source: For comparison, we calculated the corresponding FRET efficiencies from the crystal structures of the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex ( Materials and methods): the calculated FRET efficiency is 0.49 for the supercomplex between complexin-1 and the fully assembled SNARE complex (PDB ID 1KIL) and 0.13 for the complex between the superclamp mutant of complexin-1 and the partially truncated SNARE complex (PDB IDs 3RK3, 3RL0) (Chen et al., 2002; Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on crystal structures.

claim: The calculated FRET efficiency from the crystal structures PDB IDs 3RK3, 3RL0 is 0.13.
source: For comparison, we calculated the corresponding FRET efficiencies from the crystal structures of the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex ( Materials and methods): the calculated FRET efficiency is 0.49 for the supercomplex between complexin-1 and the fully assembled SNARE complex (PDB ID 1KIL) and 0.13 for the complex between the superclamp mutant of complexin-1 and the partially truncated SNARE complex (PDB IDs 3RK3, 3RL0) (Chen et al., 2002; Kümmel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on crystal structures.

claim: The cis conformation of complexin-1 corresponds to a FRET efficiency that is larger than that derived from the crystal structures.
source: Thus, the cis conformation of complexin-1 corresponds to a FRET efficiency that is larger than that derived from the crystal structures, including error estimates (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between measured FRET efficiencies and calculated values from crystal structures.

claim: The percentage of the cis conformation slightly increased for the superclamp mutant compared to wildtype complexin-1.
source: The percentage of the cis conformation slightly increased for the superclamp mutant, whereas it substantially decreased for the no-clamp mutant of complexin-1 compared to wildtye complexin-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The percentage of the cis conformation substantially decreased for the no-clamp mutant compared to wildtype complexin-1.
source: The percentage of the cis conformation slightly increased for the superclamp mutant, whereas it substantially decreased for the no-clamp mutant of complexin-1 compared to wildtye complexin-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The large effect of the no-clamp mutant on the population of the high FRET efficiency state suggests that the cis conformation of complexin-1 involves an intimate interaction of the accessory domain with the ternary SNARE complex.
source: The large effect of the no-clamp mutant on the population of the high FRET efficiency state suggests that the cis conformation of complexin-1 involves an intimate interaction of the accessory domain of complexin-1 with the ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational data.

claim: Upon addition of 1 μM full-length wildtype complexin-1, a low FRET efficiency state emerged for the SFC1 and SFC2 label pairs at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex.
source: Upon addition of 1 μM full-length wildtype complexin-1, a low FRET efficiency state emerged for the SFC1 and SFC2 label pairs at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex, but not for the SFC3 label pair at the N-terminal end (Figure 4A,B and Table 2) with occasional transitions between high and low FRET states of the SNARE complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the smFRET data shown in Figure 4A,B and Table 2.

claim: No low FRET efficiency state emerged for the SFC3 label pair at the N-terminal end upon addition of complexin-1.
source: Upon addition of 1 μM full-length wildtype complexin-1, a low FRET efficiency state emerged for the SFC1 and SFC2 label pairs at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex, but not for the SFC3 label pair at the N-terminal end (Figure 4A,B and Table 2) with occasional transitions between high and low FRET states of the SNARE complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the smFRET data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Occasional transitions between high and low FRET states of the SNARE complex were observed.
source: Upon addition of 1 μM full-length wildtype complexin-1, a low FRET efficiency state emerged for the SFC1 and SFC2 label pairs at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex, but not for the SFC3 label pair at the N-terminal end (Figure 4A,B and Table 2) with occasional transitions between high and low FRET states of the SNARE complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the time traces shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population of the low FRET efficiency state increases as the complexin-1 concentration is increased, reaching saturation around 1 μM.
source: The population of the low FRET efficiency state increases as the complexin-1 concentration is increased, reaching saturation around 1 μM within experimental error (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the concentration-dependent data shown in Figure 4C,E.

claim: At higher complexin-1 concentration there is a higher likelihood of complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex formation.
source: At higher concentration there is a higher likelihood of complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex formation consistent with the dissociation constant of this complex of around 10–100 nM (Pabst et al., 2002; Li et al., 2007), and consequently, also a higher likelihood of bound complexin-1 in the cis conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and prior knowledge of binding constants.

claim: The dissociation constant of the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex is around 10–100 nM.
source: At higher concentration there is a higher likelihood of complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex formation consistent with the dissociation constant of this complex of around 10–100 nM (Pabst et al., 2002; Li et al., 2007), and consequently, also a higher likelihood of bound complexin-1 in the cis conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The low FRET efficiency state induced by complexin-1 is different from the low FRET efficiency state observed when ternary SNAREs are assembled without the dN-SB method.
source: We note that the low FRET efficiency state that is induced by the cis conformation of complexin-1 is different from the low FRET efficiency state that is observed when ternary SNAREs are assembled without the dN-SB method (compare Figures 2C and 4B).
evidence: This is a comparison between two different experimental conditions shown in different figures.

claim: There was very little or no change in fluorescence anisotropy for all label sites in the presence of complexin-1 compared to SNARE complex without complexin-1.
source: There was very little or no change in fluorescence anisotropy for all label sites in the presence of complexin-1 compared to SNARE complex without complexin-1, suggesting that restrictions of the rotational freedoms of the dye molecules by bound complexin-1 are unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Table 3.

claim: Restrictions of the rotational freedoms of the dye molecules by bound complexin-1 are unlikely.
source: There was very little or no change in fluorescence anisotropy for all label sites in the presence of complexin-1 compared to SNARE complex without complexin-1, suggesting that restrictions of the rotational freedoms of the dye molecules by bound complexin-1 are unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference from the fluorescence anisotropy data.

claim: The sums of the donor and acceptor intensities are similar for the single molecule fluorescence intensity time traces before photobleaching occurs.
source: Moreover, the sums of the donor and acceptor intensities are similar for the single molecule fluorescence intensity time traces before photobleaching occurs (see representative time traces in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that there is no large protein induced fluorescence enhancement as seen in some systems when a protein binds near a fluorophore at short distance (Hwang and Myong, 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from the time traces shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no large protein induced fluorescence enhancement when complexin-1 binds to the SNARE complex.
source: Moreover, the sums of the donor and acceptor intensities are similar for the single molecule fluorescence intensity time traces before photobleaching occurs (see representative time traces in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that there is no large protein induced fluorescence enhancement as seen in some systems when a protein binds near a fluorophore at short distance (Hwang and Myong, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the intensity data.

claim: The low FRET efficiency state persisted after application of the γ-correction.
source: We also ruled out photo-physical effects on quantum yield and detection efficiency as an explanation for the observed appearance of the population of the low FRET efficiency state by empirically determining the γ-factor for individual molecules (Figure 5, Table 2—source data 1 and Materials and methods). The low FRET efficiency state persisted after application of the γ-correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the γ-corrected data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Measurements of binding kinetics and equilibrium binding constants for the labeled proteins agree with literature values of unlabeled proteins.
source: Finally, we note that measurements of binding kinetics and equilibrium binding constants for the labeled proteins (Materials and methods) agree with literature values of unlabeled proteins (Pabst et al., 2002), again suggesting that the fluorophores do not interfere with the binding surfaces.
evidence: This is a comparison between measured values and literature values.

claim: The fluorophores do not interfere with the binding surfaces.
source: Finally, we note that measurements of binding kinetics and equilibrium binding constants for the labeled proteins (Materials and methods) agree with literature values of unlabeled proteins (Pabst et al., 2002), again suggesting that the fluorophores do not interfere with the binding surfaces.
evidence: This is an inference from the agreement between labeled and unlabeled protein binding constants.

claim: The population of the low FRET efficiency states observed for the SNARE label pairs SFC1 and SFC2 represent a distinct conformational state of the ternary SNARE complex that is induced by complexin-1.
source: Taken together, all these controls and observations suggest that the population of the low FRET efficiency states observed for the SNARE label pairs SFC1 and SFC2 (Figure 4B) represent a distinct conformational state of the ternary SNARE complex that is induced by complexin-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including controls for dye effects.

claim: The superclamp mutant of complexin-1 slightly increased the population of the low FRET efficiency state compared to wildtype complexin-1.
source: The superclamp mutant (Figure 1A) of the accessory domain of complexin-1 slightly increased the population of the low FRET efficiency state compared to wildtype complexin-1, while the no-clamp mutant did not induce a conformational change of the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4D,F.

claim: The no-clamp mutant did not induce a conformational change of the ternary SNARE complex.
source: The superclamp mutant (Figure 1A) of the accessory domain of complexin-1 slightly increased the population of the low FRET efficiency state compared to wildtype complexin-1, while the no-clamp mutant did not induce a conformational change of the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 4D,F.

claim: The low FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the cis conformation of complexin-1 in Figure 3B.
source: Therefore the low FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the cis conformation of complexin-1 in Figure 3B, and the high FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the trans conformation of complexin-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between mutant effects in different experiments.

claim: The high FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the trans conformation of complexin-1.
source: Therefore the low FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the cis conformation of complexin-1 in Figure 3B, and the high FRET efficiency state in Figure 4B likely corresponds to the trans conformation of complexin-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between mutant effects in different experiments.

claim: The 4M mutant of complexin-1 had no effect on the ternary SNARE complex.
source: As control, we also tested the 4M mutant (Figure 1A) of complexin-1 that blocks the binding of the central domain of complexin-1 to SNARE complex and abolishes all functions of complexin-1 (Maximov et al., 2009). As expected, it had no effect on the ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a control experiment confirming that binding is required for the effect.

claim: The conformational change at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex depended on the inclusion of both the N-terminal and the accessory domains of complexin-1.
source: Finally, the conformational change at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex depended on the inclusion of both the N-terminal and the accessory domains of complexin-1 since truncation of one or both of these domains (Figure 1B) did not produce the conformational change (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the truncation mutant data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Truncation of the N-terminal or accessory domains of complexin-1 did not produce the conformational change of the SNARE complex.
source: Finally, the conformational change at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex depended on the inclusion of both the N-terminal and the accessory domains of complexin-1 since truncation of one or both of these domains (Figure 1B) did not produce the conformational change (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the truncation mutant data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: The binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complex bound weakly to the preassembled complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex via the accessory domain.
source: The binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complex bound weakly to the preassembled complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex via the accessory domain (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the binding data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: From the measured rate constants, koff = 2.16 ± 0.02 s-1 and kon = 0.34 ± 0.07 μM-1s-1, resulting in KD = 6.46 ± 1.2 μM for binding between binary SNARE complex and complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex.
source: From dwell time analysis we obtained rate constants koff = 2.16 ± 0.02 s-1 and kon = 0.34 ± 0.07 μM-1s-1, resulting in KD = 6.46 ± 1.2 μM (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The affinity between the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex and the binary SNARE complex is roughly three times weaker than that between complexin-1 and binary SNARE complex alone.
source: The affinity between the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex and the binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complex is roughly three times weaker than that between complexin-1 and binary (syntaxin-1A / SNAP-25A) SNARE complex alone (Figure 6E and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a comparison between two measured affinities.

claim: The koff rate of the superclamp mutant of complexin-1 was ~1.5-fold slower (1.36 ± 0.06 s-1) than that of wildtype complexin-1.
source: The koff rate of the superclamp mutant of complexin-1 was ~1.5-fold slower (1.36 ± 0.06 s-1) than that of wildtype complexin-1, while the kon was ~1.5-fold faster (0.56 ± 0.06 μM-1s-1), resulting in KD = 2.42 ± 0.3 μM (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The kon of the superclamp mutant was ~1.5-fold faster (0.56 ± 0.06 μM-1s-1) than that of wildtype complexin-1.
source: The koff rate of the superclamp mutant of complexin-1 was ~1.5-fold slower (1.36 ± 0.06 s-1) than that of wildtype complexin-1, while the kon was ~1.5-fold faster (0.56 ± 0.06 μM-1s-1), resulting in KD = 2.42 ± 0.3 μM (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The complexin-1 superclamp mutant interacts with the binary SNARE complex with three-fold higher affinity than wildtype complexin-1.
source: Thus, the complexin-1 superclamp mutant interacts with the binary SNARE complex with three-fold higher affinity than wildtype complexin-1.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured KD values.

claim: Binary SNARE complex binding events with the no-clamp mutant were very rare.
source: In contrast, binary SNARE complex binding events with the no-clamp mutant were very rare within our observation period of 100 s and, consequently, we were unable to determine a dissociation constant for the no-clamp mutant, consistent with the notion that it is the complexin-1 accessory domain that establishes the interaction with the binary SNARE complex in our experiment.
evidence: This is an observation from the binding experiments.

claim: It is the complexin-1 accessory domain that establishes the interaction with the binary SNARE complex.
source: In contrast, binary SNARE complex binding events with the no-clamp mutant were very rare within our observation period of 100 s and, consequently, we were unable to determine a dissociation constant for the no-clamp mutant, consistent with the notion that it is the complexin-1 accessory domain that establishes the interaction with the binary SNARE complex in our experiment.
evidence: This is an inference from the no-clamp mutant data.

claim: The 4M mutant did not bind to binary SNARE complex at all.
source: As expected, the 4M mutant did not bind at all.
evidence: This is a control experiment confirming specificity.

claim: The trans conformation of complexin-1 can bridge two SNARE complexes.
source: In summary, the trans conformation of complexin-1 can bridge two SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bridging experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Complexin-1 can bridge a ternary SNARE complex and a binary SNARE complex.
source: At variance with this previous study involving partially truncated ternary SNARE complexes (Kümmel et al., 2011), our results now show that complexin-1 can also bridge a ternary SNARE complex and a binary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the bridging experiments in Figure 6, contrasting with prior work.

claim: Previous single molecule experiments indicated the presence of improperly assembled SNAREs, including antiparallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations.
source: Previous single molecule experiments indicated the presence of improperly assembled SNAREs, including antiparallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations, when mixed in the absence of other factors that assist proper SNARE complex formation (Weninger et al., 2003; Lou et al., 2015; Ryu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Antiparallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations can be suppressed by extensive purification of the ternary SNARE complex, including an additional urea wash step.
source: As previously described (Weninger et al., 2003), antiparallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfigurations can be suppressed by extensive purification of the ternary SNARE complex, including an additional urea wash step.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The dN-SB method results in the proper parallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfiguration within the ternary SNARE complex.
source: Our smFRET experiments indicate that the dN-SB method (Pobbati et al., 2006) also results in the proper parallel syntaxin-1A / synaptobrevin-2 subconfiguration within the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: Ensemble averaging in previous FRET experiments probably masked the existence of the two populations of complexin-1 conformations.
source: We note that ensemble averaging in previous FRET experiments probably masked the existence of the two populations (Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about why prior ensemble experiments did not observe two populations.

claim: The accessory domain is important for the cis conformation of complexin-1.
source: The superclamp mutant of complexin-1 slightly increases the population of the high FRET efficiency state, while the no-clamp mutant greatly decreases the population of the high FRET efficiency state (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that the accessory domain is important for the cis conformation of complexin-1.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC NMR spectra with 15N labeled ternary SNARE complex and complexin-1 revealed interactions between the complexin-1 N-terminus with all components at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex.
source: As independent evidence for a conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex, 1H-15N TROSY-HSQC NMR spectra with 15N labeled ternary SNARE complex and complexin-1 revealed interactions between the complexin-1 N-terminus with all components (syntaxin-1A, SNAP-25A, and synaptobrevin-2) at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 5b in Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claim: Most of the spin-labeled residues of the accessory domain of complexin-1 exhibited spectral broadening when quaternary complex was formed with the SNARE complex.
source: The interaction between complexin-1 and ternary SNARE complex was also examined by EPR (Lu et al., 2010). Most of the spin-labeled residues of the accessory domain of complexin-1 exhibited spectral broadening when quaternary complex was formed with the SNARE complex, likely due to formation of an α-helical conformation of the accessory domain of complexin-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior EPR studies.

claim: The observed sharpening of EPR spectra could be due to motion between several conformations that are sampled by the accessory domain.
source: However, the authors noted that the spectra were sharper than those for solvent exposed residues on the surface of an α-helix that is part of a globular protein. Therefore, the observed sharpening could be due to motion between several conformations that are sampled by the accessory domain, consistent with the range of conformations that are suggested by our smFRET efficiency histogram (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior EPR data in light of the current smFRET data.

claim: Spin-labeling of the C-terminal half of the cytoplasmic domain of synaptobrevin-2 indicated little effect on the EPR line widths for most of the labels.
source: Spin-labeling of the C-terminal half of the cytoplasmic domain of synaptobrevin-2 indicated little effect on the EPR line widths for most of the labels (Lu et al., 2010), suggesting that the conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex does not involve a dissociation of a part of synaptobrevin-2, but rather that synaptobrevin-2 is still interacting with the other components of the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior EPR data.

claim: The conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex does not involve a dissociation of a part of synaptobrevin-2.
source: Spin-labeling of the C-terminal half of the cytoplasmic domain of synaptobrevin-2 indicated little effect on the EPR line widths for most of the labels (Lu et al., 2010), suggesting that the conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex does not involve a dissociation of a part of synaptobrevin-2, but rather that synaptobrevin-2 is still interacting with the other components of the complexin-1 / ternary SNARE supercomplex.
evidence: This is an inference from prior EPR data.

claim: The N-terminal domain (residues 1–27) of complexin-1 is important for activation of fast synchronous Ca2+-triggered release and it interacts with the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex.
source: The N-terminal domain (residues 1–27) of complexin-1 is important for activation of fast synchronous Ca2+-triggered release and it interacts with the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex (Xue et al., 2007, 2010; Maximov et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cis conformation of complexin-1 is related to activation of Ca2+-triggered release.
source: Since we have shown that the cis conformation of complexin-1 induces a conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex through a mechanism that involves both the accessory and the N-terminal domains of complexin-1, we speculate that the cis conformation of complexin-1 is related to activation of Ca2+-triggered release, although it could also play a role in regulation of spontaneous release (Giraudo et al., 2006; 2009) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Mutations of the accessory domain of complexin-1 do not affect the activating function of complexin-1 compared to wildtype neurons in rescue experiments with complexin-1 knockdown.
source: However, we note that mutations of the accessory domain of complexin-1 do not affect the activating function of complexin-1 compared to wildtype neurons in rescue experiments with complexin-1 knockdown (Yang et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuronal studies.

claim: The interaction of the N-terminal domain of complexin-1 occurs for the trans SNARE complex that is juxtaposed between the membranes regardless of the accessory domain.
source: These observations can be reconciled with the findings in this work by postulating that the interaction of the N-terminal domain of complexin-1 occurs for the trans SNARE complex that is juxtaposed between the membranes regardless of the accessory domain.
evidence: This is a speculative model to reconcile different observations.

claim: When starting from fully assembled ternary SNARE complex, both the accessory and N-terminal domains are required to induce the observed conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex.
source: In contrast when starting from fully assembled ternary SNARE complex, both the accessory and N-terminal domains are required to induce the observed conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the truncation mutant data.

claim: The complexin-1 induced conformation of the SNARE complex may be related to the conformation of a trans SNARE complex that juxtaposes the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes.
source: We speculate that the complexin-1 induced conformation of the SNARE complex may be related to the conformation of a trans SNARE complex that juxtaposes the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes (Figure 7, right panel).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: One complexin-1 molecule in the trans conformation can bridge a variety of SNARE complexes.
source: Together with previous results (Kümmel et al., 2011), one complexin-1 molecule in the trans conformation can bridge a variety of SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion combining current data with prior literature.

claim: The bridging interaction between complexin-1 and binary SNARE complex is probably specific rather than merely a consequence of the flexible character of the binary SNARE complex.
source: The correlations between complexin-1 mutants and this bridging interaction (Figure 6C–E) suggests that it is probably specific rather than merely a consequence of the flexible character of the binary SNARE complex that may expose hydrophobic elements in certain configurations (Weninger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational data and prior knowledge.

claim: The trans conformation of complexin-1 is related to regulation of spontaneous fusion.
source: We speculate that the trans conformation of complexin-1 is related to regulation of spontaneous fusion (Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011) (Figure 7, left panel).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The two previously proposed SNARE complex 'clamping' models are not mutually exclusive.
source: Our results also suggest that the two previously proposed SNARE complex 'clamping' models (Giraudo et al., 2006, 2009; Krishnakumar et al., 2011; Kümmel et al., 2011) are not mutually exclusive (see both panels in Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data showing two conformations.

claim: A conformational change at the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex has been independently observed upon αSNAP binding to ternary SNARE complex by smFRET experiments.
source: A conformational change at the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex has been independently observed upon αSNAP binding to ternary SNARE complex by smFRET experiments with labels attached to synaptobrevin-2 and SNAP-25A (Ryu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior smFRET studies.

claim: A low FRET population was induced by αSNAP that increased as the αSNAP concentration was increased.
source: Similar to the complexin-1 induced conformational change at the C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex that we observe, a low FRET population was induced by αSNAP that increased as the αSNAP concentration was increased (compare Figure S4B in [Ryu et al., 2015] with Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature.

claim: No conformational change was observed at the N-terminal end of the SNARE complex upon αSNAP binding.
source: In contrast, no conformational change was observed at the N-terminal end of the SNARE complex upon αSNAP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The C-terminal end of the SNARE complex has different conformational properties than the N-terminal end.
source: Since two quite different factors (complexin-1 and αSNAP) can induce a conformational change at the C-terminal end of the SNARE complex, this suggests that the C-terminal end has different conformational properties than the N-terminal end.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of complexin-1 and αSNAP effects.

claim: The observed plasticity of the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex likely has a functional role in membrane fusion.
source: Taken together, the observed plasticity of the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex likely has a functional role in membrane fusion, and the N-terminal domain of complexin-1 assists this process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The N-terminal domain of complexin-1 assists the process of membrane fusion.
source: Taken together, the observed plasticity of the membrane-proximal C-terminal end of the ternary SNARE complex likely has a functional role in membrane fusion, and the N-terminal domain of complexin-1 assists this process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: For the complexin-1 interaction with the ternary SNARE complex, the koff and kon rate constants were 0.12 ± 0.03 s-1 and 1.62 ± 0.1 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 0.07 ± 0.01 μM.
source: For the complexin-1 interaction with the ternary SNARE complex, the koff and kon rate constants were 0.12 ± 0.03 s-1 and 1.62 ± 0.1 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 0.07 ± 0.01 μM (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 8F-H.

claim: These values agree reasonably well with previous single molecule measurements with ternary SNARE complex that used reconstituted full length syntaxin-1A.
source: These values agree reasonably well with previous single molecule measurements with ternary SNARE complex that used reconstituted full length syntaxin-1A (Li et al., 2007), validating the surface-tethering method used in this work.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature to validate the method.

claim: For the complexin-1 interaction to the binary SNARE complex the koff and kon rate constants were 1.8 ± 0.07 s-1 and 0.92 ± 0.03 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 2.0 ± 0.03 μM.
source: For the complexin-1 interaction to the binary SNARE complex the koff and kon rate constants were 1.8 ± 0.07 s-1 and 0.92 ± 0.03 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 2.0 ± 0.03 μM, in good agreement with previous isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments (KD = 2.4 ± 0.2 μM, ref. [Li et al., 2011]).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements and comparison with prior ITC data.

claim: For the complexin-1 interaction to syntaxin-1A alone, the koff and kon rates constants were 2.96 ± 0.44 s-1 and 0.16 ± 0.001 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 18.5 ± 2.8 μM.
source: For the complexin-1 interaction to syntaxin-1A alone, the koff and kon rates constants were 2.96 ± 0.44 s-1 and 0.16 ± 0.001 μM-1s-1, respectively, resulting in KD = 18.5 ± 2.8 μM.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements.

claim: Complexin-1 has a weak affinity to syntaxin-1A alone, and binds progressively more strongly from binary to ternary SNARE complex.
source: In summary, complexin-1 has a weak affinity to syntaxin-1A alone, and binds progressively more strongly from binary to ternary SNARE complex (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is a summary of the binding affinity measurements.

claim: The kinetic rate constants of both the superclamp and no-clamp mutants were similar to that of wildtype complexin-1 for binding to ternary SNARE complex.
source: The kinetic rate constants of both the superclamp and no-clamp mutants were similar to that of wildtype complexin-1, resulting in KD = 0.063 ± 0.01 μM and 0.068 ± 0.01 μM, respectively (Figure 8I–K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 8I-K.

claim: The kon rate for the complexin-1 4M mutant was not measurable on the time scale of the experiment.
source: As expected, the kon rate for the complexin-1 4M mutant was not measurable on the time scale of our experiment, and koff rate was 1.34 ± 0.01 s-1, which is more than 10 times weaker than that for wildtype complexin-1.
evidence: This is an observation from the binding experiments with the 4M mutant.

claim: The koff rate for the 4M mutant was 1.34 ± 0.01 s-1, which is more than 10 times weaker than that for wildtype complexin-1.
source: As expected, the kon rate for the complexin-1 4M mutant was not measurable on the time scale of our experiment, and koff rate was 1.34 ± 0.01 s-1, which is more than 10 times weaker than that for wildtype complexin-1.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the kinetic measurements.

claim: The lack of an effect of the no-clamp and superclamp mutants on the affinity between complexin-1 and SNARE complex suggests that the binding is dominated by the interaction between the core domain of complexin-1 and ternary SNARE complex.
source: The lack of an effect of the no-clamp and superclamp mutants on the affinity between complexin-1 and SNARE complex suggests that under the particular conditions of this experiment, the binding is dominated by the interaction between the core domain of complexin-1 and ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutational data.
